title: Python Basics — Lecture 1
description: A question bank based on the uploaded 12-page lecture notes, plus explicitly tagged interview-style extensions.
origin: Apna College — Python Notes (Lecture 1), uploaded PDF

options: Writing instructions that a computer can execute
questions.explanation: Programming means specifying instructions to perform tasks. The instructions may be written in a language like Python.

questions.prompt: Which representation is ultimately understood by a processor?
questions.explanation: At the hardware level, processors execute machine instructions, commonly described using bits (0 and 1).

questions.prompt: In the lecture’s introductory model, what does a compiler do?
options: Runs each statement as soon as it is typed
Translates the whole program before running it
questions.explanation: The lecture contrasts whole-program compilation with step-by-step interpretation. Real compiler/runtime pipelines can be more nuanced.

questions.prompt: According to the lecture, Python primarily uses which execution approach?
questions.explanation: The notes introduce Python as interpreted; typical CPython also compiles Python source to bytecode first.

questions.prompt: Which sequence best matches the simplified programming diagram on page 1?
questions.explanation: The slide presents your source code passing through a translator so the computer can execute it.

questions.prompt: Which statement about CPython is more technically precise than “Python never compiles”?
options: CPython commonly compiles source to bytecode before executing it on a virtual machine
CPython produces a native executable for every script automatically
Python statements can never be parsed
questions.explanation: CPython normally compiles modules to Python bytecode for evaluation; the lecture’s interpreter comparison is a teaching simplification.

questions.prompt: Which tool actually explains how to fix a syntax error?
options: A program translator/runtime reports the error
questions.explanation: A parser/interpreter catches invalid Python syntax and reports an error; the programmer then fixes the code.

questions.prompt: What happens to a Python file containing invalid syntax before execution begins in normal CPython module execution?
options: Statements before the error always run
The file cannot be compiled, so no top-level statements in that module execute
Only the invalid line is ignored
questions.explanation: The module is compiled before its top-level code is executed; SyntaxError prevents module execution. This refines the line-by-line simplification.
Guido van Rossum created Python.

questions.prompt: What does “high-level language” mean in the context of the notes?
options: You must manually control each CPU register
It abstracts many low-level hardware and memory details
questions.explanation: High-level code lets programmers focus on algorithms rather than most machine-specific details.

questions.prompt: Which operating systems are explicitly mentioned as Python targets?
questions.explanation: The notes call Python portable across Windows, macOS and Linux.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Python licensing is correct?
options: It is free and open source
Every use requires a license fee
questions.explanation: The notes describe Python as free and open source.

questions.prompt: What is a benefit of Python’s readable syntax?
options: It can make programs easier to read and learn
It converts every string to a number
questions.explanation: Readability helps people learn and maintain code; it does not eliminate bugs.

questions.prompt: Does “portable” guarantee a Python program behaves identically on every computer?
options: Yes, including filesystem paths and installed packages
No; platform APIs, installed packages and environmental details can still differ
Only if all variables are integers
Yes, even without a Python interpreter
questions.explanation: Many programs are portable, but external dependencies, paths and OS-specific APIs can affect behavior.

questions.prompt: Which statement about memory in Python is accurate?
options: Python manages most memory automatically, although programs still consume memory
All Python objects are stored permanently
questions.explanation: Python abstracts manual allocation for everyday code but still creates and holds objects in memory.

questions.prompt: What is the output of this code?
questions.explanation: The quotes delimit a string literal; print outputs its contents.
The arithmetic expression is evaluated before print displays it.
By default print separates comma-separated arguments with a space.

questions.prompt: Which line correctly prints the numeric value 23 without using a string?
questions.explanation: print(23) displays the integer. The second option is unclosed, the third is a comment, and the fourth assigns a new variable.

questions.prompt: What is the default separator between multiple print arguments?
questions.explanation: The sep parameter defaults to one space.
sep="-" replaces the default separating space.

questions.prompt: How many lines of output does this produce?
questions.explanation: end="" suppresses the newline after the first print call.
Passing one list object prints its string representation, including the brackets.
print writes to standard output and returns None.

questions.prompt: When given a normal string, what does print do with quote marks used as delimiters?
questions.explanation: Quotation marks identify source-code string literals but do not appear as part of the string value.

questions.prompt: Which list contains only Python character categories mentioned in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The notes cover letters, digits, symbols, whitespace and Unicode characters.
Tabs and newlines are examples of whitespace.

questions.prompt: Which is a special symbol used in Python?
questions.explanation: The list on page 2 explicitly includes symbols such as +, -, *, / and %. Other symbols can be part of string data.

questions.prompt: Can a Python string contain an emoji?
options: Yes, strings can hold Unicode characters
questions.explanation: Python 3 text strings hold Unicode, so emoji and other non-ASCII characters are supported.

questions.prompt: Which escape sequence normally represents a newline inside a Python string?
questions.explanation: \n represents the newline character inside an ordinary Python string.

questions.prompt: Is the Unicode identifier café valid in Python 3?
options: Yes, many Unicode letters are valid identifiers
questions.explanation: Python 3 identifiers can include many Unicode letters; the basic ASCII-focused rules in the lecture are a simplified introduction.
ord returns the Unicode code point as an integer. Capital A has code point 65.

questions.prompt: Which operator assigns a value to a name?
questions.explanation: Single equals assigns a reference/value to a variable; == compares two values.
The second assignment updates age to 24.
The variable x stores the value 5.
y receives 5, then x changes independently to 8.

questions.prompt: What does a name refer to in Python?
options: A fixed physical RAM address visible to the programmer
A CPU register chosen by the user
questions.explanation: At a conceptual level, assignment binds a name to an object; memory-location language in beginner notes is an analogy.

questions.code:
a = 1
b = 2
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)
questions.explanation: Tuple unpacking evaluates the right side before assigning both names.
Both names initially reference the integer 3; a += 1 rebinds a to 4 rather than changing b.

questions.prompt: Why is sum = 5 technically legal but generally discouraged?
options: It shadows the built-in sum function
questions.explanation: sum is the name of a built-in function, not a Python keyword. Reusing it as a variable shadows that built-in in the current scope.

questions.prompt: Which statement updates an already defined variable?
questions.explanation: Assignments can rebind an existing variable; == is a comparison.
Using a name that has not been defined in the current accessible scope raises NameError.

questions.prompt: Which is a valid variable name?
questions.explanation: An underscore is allowed; spaces, hyphens and a starting digit are not.

questions.prompt: Can an identifier begin with a digit?
options: Only if it has an underscore after the digit
questions.explanation: Names cannot begin with digits.

questions.prompt: How does Python treat score and Score?
questions.explanation: Identifiers are case-sensitive.

questions.prompt: Which character is allowed in the middle of a normal identifier?
questions.explanation: The underscore is a valid character in an identifier.
for is a reserved keyword and cannot be assigned as a name.
An identifier may begin with underscores; @, dots and spaces cannot be used in a single identifier.
Letters, underscores and digits (not at the start) can be combined.

questions.prompt: Which standard-library function checks whether a string can be a Python identifier?
questions.explanation: str.isidentifier() recognizes identifier syntax, but it does not reject Python keywords.
The method tests identifier *shape*; for is syntactically an identifier but is reserved as a keyword.

questions.prompt: Which test identifies reserved keywords reliably?
questions.explanation: The keyword module provides iskeyword, used with a string name.
Whole-number literals such as 42 are integers.
Decimal floating-point literals are float values.
Quotes make "42" text rather than a numeric integer.
Python’s Boolean literal spellings are True and False.
None is the singleton value representing absence of a value, and type(None) is NoneType.
type(10) gives the int type object.
The j suffix denotes an imaginary component; the literal yields a complex number.
None is an instance of the built-in NoneType.

options: bool is a subclass of int in Python
questions.explanation: For compatibility, bool subclasses int, so True behaves numerically like 1 in some arithmetic.
True is numerically 1; adding two True values yields the integer 2.
For number comparison, Boolean True equals integer 1.
bool subclasses int, so isinstance(True, int) is True; type(True) is bool.

questions.prompt: What is the value of type(False).__name__?
questions.explanation: The exact built-in type name is bool.

questions.prompt: Which is the recommended test to check for absence of a value?
questions.explanation: None is a singleton; identity testing with is None is idiomatic.

options: A reserved word with special language meaning
questions.explanation: Keywords are language-reserved and not valid variable names.
return is reserved; print and sum are built-ins but not keywords.

questions.prompt: Which capitalization is correct for the Boolean keyword?
questions.explanation: The Python literal is True with an uppercase T.

questions.prompt: Which set contains only reserved keywords?
questions.explanation: if, for and while are control-flow keywords; the other sets contain built-in names.

questions.prompt: Which name is NOT a reserved keyword?
questions.explanation: input is a built-in function, while None, False and lambda are reserved words.

questions.prompt: Which word starts with a capital letter when written as a Python literal?
questions.explanation: True, False and None are capitalized; most other keywords are lowercase.

questions.prompt: What happens if you run the following?
questions.explanation: True is a keyword/literal and cannot be used as an assignment target.

questions.prompt: Which expression is a valid use of the keyword operator is?
questions.explanation: is is an identity-comparison operator, not an assignable variable or callable function.
keyword.iskeyword checks whether a string is a reserved word.

questions.code:
a = 5
b = 10
print("Sum is", a + b)
questions.explanation: + adds two integers and print displays the result.

questions.prompt: Which operator is best for finding the area of a square from its side length?
questions.explanation: Area of a square is side × side, or side ** 2.

questions.prompt: What is the mean of 4.5 and 7.5?
Which formula correctly computes the average of a and b?
questions.explanation: Parentheses ensure you divide the *sum* by 2 rather than dividing only b.
10 is greater than or equal to 7; a >= b is a Boolean expression.
Division happens before subtraction: 6 / 2 is 3.0, and 10 - 3.0 is 7.0.
(3 + 5) / 4 is 2.0, and int(2.0) gives 2.

questions.prompt: Which character starts a single-line comment?
questions.explanation: Python uses # to start a comment outside a string.
The comment is ignored and the print statement runs.

options: Yes, a trailing # comment is allowed
No, comments must be on their own line
questions.explanation: A # comment may follow an executable statement on the same line.

questions.prompt: What does # mean inside a quoted string?
questions.explanation: Comment syntax is not recognized inside a string literal.

questions.prompt: How are triple quotes used in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The PDF illustrates multi-line notes using triple-quoted text.

questions.prompt: What is technically true of an unassigned triple-quoted block?
options: It is a special token that Python erases in all contexts
It is a string literal expression, commonly used as a docstring in certain positions
It is always a syntax error
questions.explanation: The notes call it a multiline comment, but triple quotes actually create a string. At the start of a module/function/class it can become a docstring.
The # is enclosed in quotes so it is literal data, not a comment.

questions.prompt: Which statement prints the text /* hi */?
questions.explanation: C-style comment markers are not Python comment syntax; you can print them as ordinary characters.
+ is arithmetic addition.
- is subtraction.
* multiplies operands.
The / operator performs true division, producing a float for built-in integers.
% gives the remainder; 10 = 3×3 + 1.
** exponentiates: 2³ = 8.
== compares values; = assigns a value.
!= is true only when the two values differ.
Greater than or equal to includes equality.
8 is neither less than nor equal to 3.

options: Adds 5 to x and reassigns the result
Always creates a new variable named +=
questions.explanation: Augmented assignment corresponds approximately to x = x + 5 for immutable numeric x.
Boolean and returns True only when both values are truthy.
Boolean or is truthy when at least one condition is truthy.
not reverses truth value and always returns a bool.

questions.prompt: After this code, what is num?
questions.code:
num = 10
num += 5
num *= 2
num -= 10
num **= 2
print(num)

questions.explanation: Both comparisons are true, so their and result is True.
3 is not greater than 5; since both sides are False, or returns False.
not has lower precedence than comparisons: not (2 == 3) is True.
Integer floor division // discards fractional part toward negative infinity. 15 // 2 = 7.

questions.prompt: Which update is equivalent to x %= 3?
questions.explanation: %= assigns the modulo result back to x.

questions.prompt: Which update is equivalent to x /= 2?
questions.explanation: /= uses true division, so a numerical integer often becomes a float.
8 / 2 is 4.0, then assigning via /= produces a float.
Python chains comparisons: 1 < 2 < 3 tests both 1 < 2 and 2 < 3.
7 divided by 4 leaves a remainder of 3.

questions.prompt: Which operator has higher precedence among + and *?
questions.explanation: Multiplication occurs before addition, absent parentheses.
Exponentiation is right-associative: 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 2 ** 9 = 512.
Exponentiation binds more tightly than unary minus on the left: -(3 ** 2) = -9.
Parentheses make -3 the base of the power, giving (-3)² = 9.
Floor division rounds toward negative infinity, so -7 // 3 = -3.
Modulo has the divisor’s sign when the divisor is positive: -7 = (-3)*3 + 2.
With a negative divisor, modulo’s nonzero result has a negative sign: 7 = (-3)*(-3) + (-2).
Python’s comparison chain means (1 == 1) and (1 == 2), which is False.
2 < 3 and 3 > 1 are both True: comparison chaining is supported.
and is evaluated before or: False or (True and True) => True.
not binds more tightly than and and or: (not False) and (False or True) = True.
not applies to the comparison result, so not (1 < 2) is False.

questions.prompt: What is the result of 0 or 5?
questions.explanation: or returns one of its operands, not necessarily a bool: 0 is falsy, so it returns 5.

questions.prompt: What is the result of 3 and 9?
questions.explanation: and returns the last operand if all operands are truthy.

questions.prompt: What is the result of "" or "fallback"?
questions.explanation: An empty string is falsy, so or returns the nonempty right operand.

questions.prompt: What is the result of [] and 42?
questions.explanation: The empty list is falsy, and and returns that first falsy operand without evaluating the other.
The left operand of and is falsy, so the right expression is never evaluated.
True or ... short-circuits before division by zero.

questions.code:
a = None
b = 0
print(a is b)
questions.explanation: is checks object identity, not equality. None and 0 are different objects.

questions.prompt: Which expression is safest for numeric equality?
questions.explanation: Use == for value equality. Identity via is is not reliable for comparing numeric values.
Floating point 0.1 + 0.2 is not represented as exactly 0.3 in binary floating point.

questions.prompt: Which comparison is commonly preferred for approximate floating-point equality?
questions.explanation: math.isclose compares floats using controlled relative/absolute tolerances.
True is 1, and the expression evaluates as 2+3=5 because 0**0 is 1 in Python. However code uses 2**3 - 3 => 5.

questions.prompt: What does 0 ** 0 evaluate to in Python?
questions.explanation: Python defines 0 ** 0 as 1 for integer exponentiation.
1 == 1 is True; not of that Boolean is False.

questions.prompt: What does implicit type conversion mean?
options: Python automatically converts a compatible type when performing an operation
questions.explanation: Implicit conversion occurs automatically, such as adding int and float.
A mixed int + float arithmetic operation yields a float.
Python does not implicitly coerce a string into an integer for addition.
The floating-point operand promotes the numeric result to float.
Mixing an int and a str with + raises TypeError.

questions.prompt: What is the result of 3 + True?
questions.explanation: Boolean True behaves like integer 1 in numeric addition.
Mixed integer and complex arithmetic produces a complex result.
Numeric comparison of integer 3 and floating 3.0 is equal in value.
A numeric float and a string do not support + together.
The / operator produces float 1.0 even if it divides two integers.

options: An automatic operation with no function call
Manually converting a value to a target type
questions.explanation: Calling int, float, str, bool, etc. explicitly converts values.
int parses a decimal integer string.
float converts 5 into floating point 5.0.
str converts numeric 100 into textual "100".
"hello" is not a decimal integer literal, so int raises ValueError.
int("2") converts the string to an integer, so 1+2=3.
The division and int conversion can produce 5.0 here because float(5) is 5.0.
The empty string is falsy; bool returns False.
Any nonempty string is truthy, even a string spelled "False".
Numeric zero is falsy.
"0" is a nonempty string, hence truthy.
ord returns the Unicode code point; uppercase A is 65.
hex returns a string with the 0x prefix.
Octal 10 represents decimal 8; oct prefixes its string with 0o.

questions.prompt: What is the result of list("cat")?
questions.explanation: list iterates the string and collects individual characters.

questions.prompt: What is the result of tuple([1, 2])?
questions.explanation: tuple creates an immutable ordered tuple from the iterable.

questions.prompt: What is the value of len(set([2, 2, 3]))?
questions.explanation: Sets contain unique elements, so the duplicates collapse to {2, 3}.
dict can construct a dictionary from a sequence of key/value pairs.
Casting float to int truncates toward zero, it does not round.
int truncates toward zero; -3.9 becomes -3.
A decimal-point string is not a valid integer literal for direct int parsing. float("3.5") succeeds.
Parsing base 2 makes 101₂ = 1×4 + 0×2 + 1 = 5.
The base-16 string 0xff represents decimal 255.
complex(real, imag) builds the number 2+3j.
An empty list is falsy.
str represents None as the text "None".
IEEE binary floating point stores 0.1+0.2 as a nearby number, not the exact float value for 0.3.

questions.prompt: What is round(2.675, 2) in typical Python 3?
questions.explanation: Floating point 2.675 is represented slightly below the exact decimal, and round returns 2.67.
Python uses round-to-nearest with ties-to-even for exact ties, so round(2.5) = 2.
For exact halves, Python rounds to the nearest even integer, so 3.5 → 4.
None cannot be converted directly to an integer with int.
int accepts underscores between digits in numeric strings.
chr is the inverse of ord for a valid Unicode code point.

questions.prompt: What is the return type of input()?
questions.explanation: input returns a string for keyboard text.

questions.prompt: Which expression reads an integer from the keyboard?
questions.explanation: input reads a string; int then converts the entered digits to an integer.

questions.prompt: Which expression reads a floating-point number?
questions.explanation: float(input()) converts the entered text to a floating-point number.

questions.prompt: Given user input 18, what is the type of age?
questions.explanation: Even numeric-looking input is a string until converted.

questions.prompt: If the user types 18, what is printed?
questions.explanation: int converts the entered string "18" to 18, then +1 gives 19.

questions.prompt: If a user types 12 and then 8, what is printed?
questions.code:
a = int(input())
b = int(input())
print(a + b)
questions.explanation: Both values are converted to int before addition.

questions.prompt: If the user enters 5, what is the area printed?
questions.explanation: float(input()) makes 5.0, and 5.0 * 5.0 = 25.0.

questions.prompt: If input lines are 4.5 and 7.5, what does this print?
questions.code:
a = float(input())
b = float(input())
print((a + b) / 2)

questions.prompt: What is printed if a=10 and b=7 are entered?
questions.code:
a = int(input())
b = int(input())
print(a >= b)
questions.explanation: Integer 10 >= integer 7 evaluates to True.

questions.prompt: What happens if you type hello in int(input())?
questions.explanation: Parsing nonnumeric user text as an int raises ValueError.

options: The computer always adds extra tax
Binary floating-point representation introduces small rounding artifacts
questions.explanation: Many decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly in binary floating point.

questions.prompt: Which function rounds a numeric float value to two decimal places (without guaranteeing two visible trailing digits)?
questions.explanation: round(value, 2) computes a rounded number. Fixed display padding can also be done with formatting.

questions.prompt: If input returns "10", what does input() + input() print when both entries are 10?
questions.code:
a = input()
b = input()
print(a + b)
questions.explanation: Both calls return strings, and string + concatenates them.

questions.prompt: If the user enters a blank line, what is the result of int(input())?
questions.explanation: int("") fails because an empty string is not a valid integer representation.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly prints a price with exactly two digits after the decimal point?
questions.explanation: An f-string format specification .2f gives a fixed two-decimal display (including trailing zeroes).

questions.prompt: What should a program typically do when converting uncertain user input?
questions.explanation: Input validation or a try/except ValueError prevents unhandled crashes for invalid text.

questions.prompt: What exception can input() raise on end-of-file without a line?
questions.explanation: When no more input is available, input may raise EOFError.

questions.prompt: If a user enters the text True, what does bool(input()) evaluate to?
questions.explanation: The entered text is a nonempty string, regardless of its spelling; all nonempty strings are truthy.

challenges.title: Discount plus tax
challenges.prompt: Read a price, discount percentage, and tax percentage (one per line). Apply discount first, then tax. Print the final amount rounded to two decimals.
challenges.starter:
price = float(input())
discount = float(input())
tax = float(input())
challenges.hint: final = price * (1 - discount/100) * (1 + tax/100).
challenges.solution:

discount = float(input())
tax = float(input())
final = price * (1 - discount / 100) * (1 + tax / 100)

challenges.title: Even, odd and sign
challenges.prompt: Read an integer. Print `even positive`, `odd negative`, or analogous label for its parity and sign; zero should print `even zero`.
challenges.hint: Use % 2 for parity; use if/elif/else for sign.
challenges.solution:
n = int(input())
parity = "even" if n % 2 == 0 else "odd"
sign = "positive" if n > 0 else "negative" if n < 0 else "zero"
print(parity, sign)
challenges.rubric: Test the supplied examples and at least one edge case in VS Code. Mark “Solved” only when your code works without copying the solution.

challenges.title: Truthiness classifier
challenges.prompt: Read text. Print whether the input is an empty string or a nonempty string. Do NOT interpret the words False or 0 specially.
challenges.hint: bool(text) is False only when the string is empty.
challenges.solution:
text = input()
print("nonempty" if bool(text) else "empty")

challenges.title: Floating-point equality
challenges.prompt: Without hardcoding True, demonstrate that 0.1+0.2 and 0.3 are close enough using math.isclose. Print the result.
challenges.hint: Do not compare the floats with ==.
challenges.solution:
import math
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))

challenges.title: Leap-year classifier
challenges.prompt: Read a year. Print True only for Gregorian leap years (divisible by 4, except centuries must be divisible by 400).
challenges.hint: Condition: divisible by 400 OR (divisible by 4 AND not by 100).
challenges.solution:
year = int(input())
print((year % 400 == 0) or (year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0))

challenges.title: Deduplicate numeric inputs
challenges.prompt: Read a single line of comma-separated integers. Print the number of distinct integers. Ignore leading and trailing spaces around each number.
challenges.hint: split(","), strip(), int(), then set().
challenges.solution:
raw = input()
numbers = [int(part.strip()) for part in raw.split(",")]
print(len(set(numbers)))

challenges.title: Invoice total with rounding
challenges.prompt: Read quantity as int, unit price as float, and tax percentage as float. Print the invoice total prefixed with `₹` with exactly two decimal digits.
challenges.starter:
qty = int(input())
unit_price = float(input())
tax_pct = float(input())
challenges.hint: Compute qty * unit_price * (1 + tax_pct / 100), then format to .2f.
challenges.solution:
qty = int(input())
unit_price = float(input())
tax_pct = float(input())
total = qty * unit_price * (1 + tax_pct / 100)
print(f"₹{total:.2f}")

challenges.title: Short-circuit safety
challenges.prompt: Read the string on one line. Print True only if it is nonempty AND its first character is a digit, without ever raising IndexError for an empty string.
challenges.hint: and short-circuits. Use text and text[0].isdigit(), wrapped with bool if needed.
challenges.solution:
text = input()
print(bool(text and text[0].isdigit()))

challenges.title: Is a number nearly an integer?
challenges.prompt: Read one float. Print True if it differs from the nearest integer by no more than 1e-9, otherwise False.
challenges.hint: Use abs(value-round(value)) <= 1e-9. Avoid direct float comparison.
challenges.solution:
value = float(input())
print(abs(value - round(value)) <= 1e-9)
